name: Naples
info: Naples is a port city on the Gulf of Naples in southern Italy, founded by Greeks as Parthenope in the 8th century BCE and refounded as Neapolis, and for centuries the capital of the kingdoms of Naples and the Two Sicilies.

facts.founded: A Greek settlement called Parthenope was established on the coast in the 8th century BCE, and in the 6th century BCE it was refounded as Neapolis, in 507 BCE by Cumaean aristocrats expelled by the tyrant Aristodemus, as one account dates it.
facts.where: On the Gulf of Naples on the western coast of southern Italy, between Mount Vesuvius and the Phlegraean Fields, in the region of Campania.
facts.known: A Greek colony of Magna Graecia; its alliance with and later absorption by Rome; the Duchy of Naples; capital of the Kingdom of Naples and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies; the Baroque painters and the opera of the 17th and 18th centuries; the university founded in 1224; the Four Days of Naples of 1943
facts.today: Naples is the capital of the region of Campania and the third-largest city in Italy, and its historic centre has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1995.

t: Naples began as the Greek colony of Parthenope in the 8th century BCE and was refounded as Neapolis, and it kept its Greek language and customs after it came under Rome.
It was the capital of the Duchy of Naples, then of the Kingdom of Naples from 1282, and finally of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies until Italian unification in 1861.
Under Spanish rule it became one of the largest cities in Europe and a centre of Baroque art, until a plague in 1656 killed about half of its inhabitants.
dyk: In 1943 the people of Naples rose against the German occupation, and Colonel Scholl, the German commander, negotiated a surrender to the insurgents; the city was already free when British and American forces entered it on 1 October.
ev: Greeks from Cumae found Parthenope on the Pizzofalcone hill
The city is refounded as Neapolis by Cumaean aristocrats
Rome besieges Neapolis, which surrenders after a siege of a year
Belisarius takes the city for the Byzantine Empire by entering through an aqueduct
The last duke surrenders to Roger II and Naples joins the Kingdom of Sicily
Charles of Anjou moves the capital of the kingdom from Palermo to Naples
A plague kills about half of the city's inhabitants
Naples becomes part of the Kingdom of Italy

sections.origins:
Naples stands on the Gulf of Naples between two volcanic regions, Mount Vesuvius and the Phlegraean Fields. The area has been inhabited since the Neolithic period, and traces of the Serra d'Alto culture were found near the basilica of Santa Maria degli Angeli a Pizzofalcone, with later finds from the Chalcolithic and Bronze Age. In the second millennium BCE a first Mycenaean settlement arose not far from the site of the future Parthenope.

Sailors from Rhodes probably founded a small commercial port called Parthenope on the island of Megaride in the ninth century BCE. Cumae, the earliest Greek city on mainland Italy, expanded the settlement in the 8th century BCE to include the Pizzofalcone promontory and Monte Echia, where it could control sea traffic. It was named after a siren of Greek mythology who was said to have washed ashore at Megaride after failing to bewitch Ulysses. Little archaeology of Parthenope has come to light, though a necropolis of the 7th century BCE was found in via Nicotera.

The city was refounded as Neapolis, the New City, in the 6th century BCE, and one account dates this to 507 BCE, by the Cumaean aristocracy expelled by the tyrant Aristodemus. The oligarchs planned a second Cumae and kept its cults and its organisation. The old settlement became Palaipolis, the old city. Neapolis was laid out on a rectangular grid on a plateau, and swamps limited its farmland and turned it towards the sea and trade.
sections.growth:
Neapolis became one of the foremost cities of Magna Graecia. Its trade grew as the tyranny of the Deinomenids at Syracuse declined after 466 BCE, and it occupied Ischia when the Syracusan garrison left. Athens built a network of trade in the Tyrrhenian Sea, to the benefit of the port, until the Athenian expedition against Syracuse failed in 413 BCE and ties weakened. At the end of the 5th century BCE Neapolis admitted Oscan elites to public office to keep its independence from the Samnites, and it took in many refugees from Cumae after that city fell in 421 BCE.

Under Roman rule the city kept its Greek language, institutions and customs and was expanded with villas, aqueducts and public baths. From 199 BCE Puteoli replaced it as a maritime power, and it declined further after it backed the losing side in the civil wars. Under Augustus it recovered as a centre of Hellenistic culture, and in 2 CE he founded the Isolympic Games there, which he attended in 14 CE. Emperors such as Claudius and Tiberius holidayed in the area, and Virgil studied there.

Under Spanish rule Naples became one of the largest cities in Europe. It was a centre of the Baroque, home to Caravaggio, Salvator Rosa and Bernini and to the philosophers Telesio, Bruno, Campanella and Vico. Pedro Álvarez de Toledo, the most important of the viceroys, paved roads, strengthened and expanded the walls and put up fortresses and buildings. After the cholera of 1884 the city was rebuilt in part under the risanamento, which gave it the Galleria Umberto I and the Corso Umberto.
sections.rulers:
Neapolis was an ally of Rome against Carthage and was taken by the Samnites before the Romans captured it. In 326 BCE the consul Publilius Philo besieged it, and after a siege of a year it surrendered through betrayal by Greek citizens. It became a Roman municipium and held Roman rule until the fifth century, when the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was exiled to a villa on the islet of Megaride. The Ostrogoths held the city until Belisarius took it for the Byzantine Empire in 536. Totila took it in 543 and treated it leniently, and it later came under imperial rule again.

The Duchy of Naples arose under Byzantine authority, and a local duke, Basilius, ruled it from 661. Duke Stephen II turned its allegiance from Constantinople to the Pope, and the duchy was independent in practice from 840. Sergius VII surrendered to Roger II of Sicily in 1137, and Naples joined the Kingdom of Sicily. The Hohenstaufen, under Henry VI, conquered the kingdom in 1194, and Charles of Anjou made Naples its capital in 1266.

After the Sicilian Vespers the Angevins kept the mainland as the Kingdom of Naples. Alfonso of Aragon conquered the city in 1442. Spain won it from the French in 1503 and ruled it through viceroys until 1714, when Austria took it. In 1734 Charles of Bourbon made it the capital of an independent kingdom. Napoleon conquered it in 1806, and his brother Joseph and then Joachim Murat reigned there. The Bourbons returned in 1815, the kingdom became the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, and Garibaldi's forces ended its rule in 1860.
sections.life:
Neapolis kept the Greek language and customs of its founders long after Rome absorbed it. It had an acropolis, an agora, strong walls, an odeon, a theatre and a temple of its patron gods, the Dioscuri, and its grid of streets can still be seen in the historic centre. Christianity came in the Roman period. According to tradition the basilica of San Pietro ad Aram stands where Saint Peter preached and baptised the first converts, and Januarius, the city's patron saint, was martyred in 305 near Naples. Each year the Cathedral hosts the Miracle of Saint Januarius, in which his dried blood is said to turn liquid.

In the Middle Ages the duchy was ruled by an aristocracy of warriors and landowners, and in the 12th century commerce was left mainly to foreigners from Pisa and Genoa. Under the Angevins, Pisan and Genoese merchants and Tuscan bankers came, and artists such as Boccaccio, Petrarch and Giotto. Frederick II founded the University of Naples in 1224. The Naples of the early 19th century was divided between the lazzaroni, a mass of very poor and devout people who favoured the Bourbons, a royal bureaucracy and an elite of landowners.

The city also developed a tradition of music and theatre. The first music conservatories were founded under Spanish rule in the 16th century, opera buffa was created there in the 18th century, and the Teatro di San Carlo, built in 1737, has been called the oldest working theatre in Europe. The Neapolitan language is regarded as distinct from Italian, and Alfonso V stated in 1442 that it should be used in official documents in place of Latin.
sections.crises:
Naples was besieged often. In 1191 the future Henry VI laid siege to it from May to August, and disease forced his army to withdraw. The Gothic War brought the siege of 536, in which Belisarius's troops entered by the aqueduct, and Totila starved the city into surrender in 543. In 1544 Barbary corsairs took around 7,000 people from Naples as slaves.

The pressures of a crowded city exploded in July 1647 when the fisherman Masaniello led a revolt against Spanish rule. Neapolitans declared a republic and asked France for support, but the Spaniards put down the rising in April 1648. In 1656 an outbreak of bubonic plague killed about half of the city's inhabitants and began a period of decline. In 1799 French troops entered the city and a Parthenopaean Republic was proclaimed, but the royalist lazzaroni rose against it, and Horatio Nelson arrested its leaders in June and handed them over for execution.

Disease struck in the 19th century. Twelve epidemics of cholera and typhoid fever killed some 48,000 people between 1834 and 1884, and a major cholera epidemic in August 1884, blamed largely on poor sewers, led to the risanamento. Between 1876 and 1913 an estimated 4 million people emigrated from the area. Naples was the most-bombed Italian city of the Second World War. In the Four Days of Naples the people rose against the German occupation, and the departing Germans burned the university's library, destroyed the city archives and sank more than 300 ships in the harbour.
sections.legacy:
Naples left its mark in art, learning and music. The University of Naples Federico II, founded in 1224, is regarded as the oldest state-funded secular university in the world, and L'Orientale, founded in 1732 by the Jesuit Matteo Ripa, is the oldest European institution for Oriental studies. Caravaggio's arrival in 1606 was a critical factor in the Neapolitan school of painting. The city was also a centre of the Enlightenment, and its song tradition produced pieces such as 'O sole mio and Funiculì, Funiculà.

The city's buildings record its successive rulers: the Castel dell'Ovo, the Castel Nuovo built under Charles I, Castel Sant'Elmo completed in 1329, the Royal Palace and the Piazza del Plebiscito begun by Joachim Murat and finished under Ferdinand IV. The rebuilding of the church of Santa Chiara, destroyed in an American bombing raid, became the symbol of the city's rebirth after the Second World War. Beneath the city lie tunnels and cisterns dug out of the soft tuff on which much of it is built.

Naples is today the capital of Campania and the largest city in southern Italy, the third largest in Italy after Rome and Milan, with 905,050 residents within its boundaries. Its population had peaked at 1,226,594 in 1971. Its historic centre was listed by UNESCO in 1995, and the rectangular grid of the Greek foundation can still be traced in it.

summary: Naples, on the Gulf of Naples in southern Italy, began as the Greek colony of Parthenope and was refounded as Neapolis. It passed from Rome to Byzantine, Norman, Angevin, Aragonese, Spanish and Bourbon rulers and was the capital of the Kingdom of Naples until 1861.
notes: FOUNDING: the main article says Rhodian sailors probably founded Parthenope on Megaride in the 9th century BCE, then Cumaeans expanded it in the 8th; the history article says Cumae founded it at the end of the 8th century BCE. I used start -750 circa and told both accounts.
REFOUNDING: main article says 6th century BCE; history article says 507 BCE after the victory at Aricia. Both given in facts and origins.

POPULATION: 17th century about 250,000 (main) against 300,000 (history, 'from 100,000 to 300,000 under the viceroys'); both given. The plague of 1656 'about half of 300,000' (main) against 'almost half of the inhabitants' (history).

DATES that differ: Duchy of Naples lead says 661-1139 but both text sections give surrender in 1137; I used 1137. Kingdom of Naples dated 1282 (main, after the Sicilian Vespers) against 1284 (history); I used 1282 only for the split and said 'after the Sicilian Vespers' in rulers. The Four Days: 27 to 30 September (main) against 28 September to 1 October (history); I gave no dates for the rising in crises, and in dyk only 1 October for the Allied arrival, which both agree on.
Pope who crowned Charles I: Innocent IV (main) vs Clement IV (history, and the date 1266 fits Clement); I left the pope out. Charles's capital move from Palermo in 1266 is in both.

The history article says 'the Spanish regain'... the 1501 union under Aragon and Charles VIII's 1495 conquest are not in the main article; I omitted 1501-1503 details except Spain winning the city from the French in 1503 (main).
Roman 'municipium' from 199 BCE is from the history article; the main article says only that the Romans made it a colony after capturing it. I used municipium once.
Siege of 326 BCE: the history article says 'a year long siege'; the 'betrayal by Greek citizens' is its wording, kept as attributed to the siege's end.

The theatre claim ('oldest working theatre in Europe' for San Carlo) is the article's music section; the same article's palaces section says 'oldest opera house in Italy'. I wrote 'described as the oldest working theatre in Europe'.
Left out: tourism, economy, sport, transport, the Camorra, waste crisis, mayors, climate, famous living people, twin towns, film and food, as the guide requires. The pizza and cuisine are omitted.
Dyk and crises: the surrender negotiated by Colonel Scholl is the main article's account; the history article says only that the Germans were pushed out.
